title: Pentagon-Lockheed AIM-260 Deal Signals Push to Scale Classified Air-to-Air Missile as CBO Warns Two-Thirds of US Interceptor Stocks Depleted
subhead: Washington signed a framework deal to expand production of the classified AIM-260 long-range missile while a new CBO analysis says the Iran war has consumed between half and two-thirds of America's missile-defense interceptor inventory. The two developments frame the US defense industrial base's central problem: munitions are being used faster than they can be rebuilt.

sections.heading: AIM-260 'Demand Signal' Deal: A Missile Finally Comes Out of the Shadows
sections.body:
The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin signed a framework agreement on Sept. 17 to expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM), the classified long-range air-to-air weapon meant to outrange and replace the AIM-120 AMRAAM, according to Defense News. The deal is neither a contract nor an order — Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition Michael Duffey called it a 'clear, long-term demand signal' so Lockheed and its suppliers can justify investing in capacity, workforce and efficiency ahead of a future multiyear buy.

Lockheed's Tim Cahill said the company will spend its own money to expand capacity before orders arrive. The move marks one of the first times the classified program has been discussed publicly; the first external images of an AIM-260 on a Navy F/A-18F Super Hornet surfaced only in May, via The Aviationist. Reuters reported Lockheed's framing of the announcement. The missile is sized to fit the internal bays of the F-22 and F-35, with public estimates putting its range beyond 120 miles — a direct response to China's PL-15.
sections.whyItMatters: The framework-agreement model — signaling demand before committing orders — is Washington's answer to the chronic problem of munitions lines that couldn't surge when war broke out. It also pulls a previously classified missile into public view as a named export product.

sections.heading: GM Fast-Turnaround Delivers First Patriot Parts: 22 Days After Signing
sections.body:
Lockheed said it received its first shipment of housing components for PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors from GM Defense on Aug. 28 — just 22 days after the Aug. 6 contract signing, components that traditionally take months or years to produce, per Reuters via Defense News. GM Defense CEO Stephen duMont framed the automaker's precision-fabrication expertise as backing 'production of this country's critical defense capabilities.'

The effort builds on a broader June collaboration between Lockheed and GM to tap GM Defense's manufacturing plants for munitions output. Lockheed is investing $8 billion to $9 billion to scale production of PAC-3 MSE, THAAD and the Precision Strike Missile, adding buildings and jobs at more than 20 US sites with warehousing space to grow nearly 50%.
sections.whyItMatters: The 22-day turnaround is a rare concrete measure of how fast commercial manufacturing can be stood up for defense when the design and paperwork are already settled — and a sign the interceptor shortage is being treated as an industrial, not just budget, problem.

sections.heading: CBO: Iran War Cost $38 Billion, Depleted Two-Thirds of Interceptor Stocks
sections.body:
A new Congressional Budget Office analysis estimates the combat campaign against Iran has cost the US military about $38 billion through Aug. 1, and that the conflict consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the US inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025, Military Times reported. The estimate covers Patriot, THAAD, SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors combined.

CBO says the Pentagon does not disclose its interceptor inventory, so analysts compared reported expenditures against total missiles purchased. Rebuilding stocks could take at least five years even at higher production rates. Interceptors account for $13.1 billion of the $21.7 billion CBO estimates is needed to replace expended munitions; land-attack cruise missiles add $7.3 billion. CBO notes unit costs of roughly $4 million for a Patriot or SM-6, $12 million for THAAD and $28 million for an SM-3. The agency warned the depleted stocks 'could pose a particular problem in a conflict with China,' which fields large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles. A separate DoD inspector general report estimated the operation's cost at $33.4 billion through June 29.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the strategic backdrop for the AIM-260 and Patriot-GM moves: America's most expensive munitions were drawn down in a regional fight, and the inventory math for a potential China conflict is now worse than before the Iran campaign began.

sections.heading: Air Force Extends B-1, B-2 Service as B-21 Fielding Nears
sections.body:
The Air Force will extend the service lives of the B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit bombers, Gen. Stephen L. Davis, commander of Global Strike Command, said at the Air, Space & Cyber Conference, according to Defense News. Davis said experienced B-1 and B-2 pilots will be among the first to fly the B-21 Raider, which is on track for 2027 delivery to Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota, with the service aiming to field at least 100.

The extension accompanies a North Star Readiness Campaign to raise the mission-capable rate of B-52s and B-1s through faster parts delivery and depot maintenance. Davis also cited the BSTAR program, which uses XSTAR Aviation HondaJet Elite business jets to keep B-1 pilots current on flight hours amid airframe readiness issues. The commander did not specify how long the extensions will last, but both bombers had been slated for retirement within the decade.
sections.whyItMatters: Extending the legacy bomber force while the B-21 ramps is a bridge strategy — the bomber fleet's readiness and pilot pipeline must hold together until the stealth successor is operational in quantity.

sections.heading: Baltic Air Policing Tightens: Germany Sends Eurofighters; Italy Shoots Down Drone Over Lithuania
sections.body:
Germany will dispatch four Eurofighter Typhoons plus several dozen personnel to Lielvārde air base in Latvia for a week-long election-security mission in late September and early October, ahead of Latvia's Oct. 3 parliamentary vote, Defense News reported. Berlin described it as part of NATO's enhanced air policing north (eAPN), though its one-week, election-specific focus departs from routine four-month rotations.

The backdrop is rising drone anxiety on NATO's eastern flank. Italian NATO jets in neighboring Lithuania shot down a suspected Russian-made drone this week after it crossed from Belarus — the first drone downing in Lithuanian airspace. Baltic states have repeatedly flagged unauthorized drone incursions, some identified as stray Ukrainian drones and others remaining unidentified, as they press for stronger alliance commitments.
sections.whyItMatters: Air superiority in the Baltics is being redefined around drone defense, not just manned fighters — the region's vulnerability to small, hard-to-track drones is now driving real operational posture changes.

sections.heading: Japan Loses a Third of Its Global Hawk Fleet; CSIS Floats Hunting China's Carriers
sections.body:
A Japanese RQ-4B Global Hawk crashed into the Sea of Japan on Sept. 15, cutting the Japan Air Self-Defense Force's fleet by a third overnight, Defense News reported. Tokyo paid roughly $163 million per aircraft for its three Global Hawks, which track North Korean missile preparations and Chinese military activity. The JASDF lost contact at 12:55 p.m. and lost the radar signature three minutes later over international waters; the flight 'was not a training exercise,' Chief of Staff Gen. Takehiro Morita said. Japan's Maritime Self-Defense Force plans to induct the first of 23 MQ-9B SeaGuardians in 2027, with the draft 2027 budget requesting $1.88 billion for the first 17.

Separately, a CSIS report, 'Flip the Script,' argues the US and allies should target China's aircraft carriers rather than only defend against China's own carrier-killing arsenal, which includes subs, ballistic missiles and a full-scale US carrier mockup in the Taklamakan Desert, Defense News reported. CSIS contends a Fujian-class carrier loss would be as devastating politically for Beijing as losing a Ford-class carrier would be in Washington. China has three operational carriers, and a 2025 Pentagon report estimated the PLAN will build six more by 2035.
sections.whyItMatters: Long-endurance unmanned surveillance is proving fragile — Japan just lost $163M of it to a single incident — even as the region shifts to cheaper, more numerous maritime drones. The CSIS argument reframes China's carrier program as exploitable vulnerability rather than pure threat.

bottomLine: Today's theme is American munitions arithmetic. The Pentagon signed a framework deal to scale the classified AIM-260 long-range missile, General Motors delivered Patriot parts 22 days after signing, and the CBO quantified why: the Iran war consumed up to two-thirds of key interceptor stocks and costs roughly $38 billion so far, with replenishment taking at least five years. Washington is responding to the shortage the same way it responded to the drone and artillery crunches — by pulling commercial manufacturing into the munitions base and signaling demand before writing orders. Meanwhile the Air Force extended its legacy bombers to hold the line until the B-21 arrives, NATO's Baltic air policing added a drone-defeat dimension, and Japan absorbed a costly drone loss while China's carrier ambitions drew a new look-an-offense counter from CSIS. The through-line: munitions, not platforms, are now the binding constraint across every theater.
sources: Defense News, Reuters, Military Times, CBO analysis, Department of Defense inspector general report, CSIS
